posts.title: Japan Probes Major Brewers Over Suspected Price Collusion
posts.excerpt: Japan's competition watchdog has inspected major brewers over suspected price collusion. Suntory confirms an inspection and says it will cooperate.
posts.meta_description: Japan investigates Asahi, Kirin, Sapporo and Suntory over suspected price collusion. Read the confirmed events, company response and consumer context.
posts.selection_note: A developing international competition story reported on 7-8 October, supported by a first-party Suntory statement; allegation language is preserved throughout.
posts.content:
Japan's Fair Trade Commission has inspected major brewers as part of an investigation into suspected price collusion. Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Sapporo Breweries and Suntory are under investigation, according to AFP's report published by CNA. The searches took place on 7 October.

Suntory Confirms An Inspection

In its 7 October statement, Suntory Holdings says Suntory was inspected over suspected violations of Japan's anti-monopoly law relating to alcohol trading. The company says it will cooperate fully with the investigation.

What Investigators Are Examining

The AFP report describes suspicions of coordinated wholesale beer-price increases. ABC's 8 October coverage also reports the investigation and says the four companies separately expressed their intention to cooperate.

The distinction matters: an investigation is not a finding that the companies broke the law. The confirmed event is the inspection; alleged coordination is what authorities are examining.

What Beer Buyers Should Take From The News

Our reading is that this story concerns commercial pricing conduct in Japan. It should not be treated as a notice of changed Indian retail prices, a product recall or an immediate shortage in Indian shops.

For a purchase in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, compare the exact beer, pack size and local listing. For the investigation itself, follow subsequent findings and company statements. A familiar brand name makes the story relevant to drinkers, but it does not turn an allegation into a verdict.

posts.title: Lofted Spirits Names Nick Smith Master Distiller
posts.excerpt: Nick Smith takes production leadership at Lofted Spirits while Steve Nally becomes Master Distiller Emeritus; Bardstown also marks its millionth barrel.
posts.meta_title: Nick Smith Named Lofted Spirits Master Distiller | BevOry
posts.meta_description: Lofted Spirits appoints Nick Smith as master distiller. Read Steve Nally's new role, the brands involved and Bardstown's million-barrel milestone.
posts.selection_note: A 7 October company announcement with named production responsibilities and a dated milestone, adding a distinct bourbon-industry story to the regulatory news.
posts.content:
Lofted Spirits has named Nick Smith master distiller, with responsibility for production at Bardstown Bourbon Company, Green River Whiskey and Lofted Custom Spirits. The company announced the appointment on 7 October in a release carried by the Kentucky Distillers' Association. Steve Nally moves into the role of Master Distiller Emeritus.

A Handover Between Longtime Colleagues

Smith joined Bardstown Bourbon Company in 2016 after beginning his distilling career at Jim Beam. He has worked alongside Nally for the past decade. Nally will continue as an ambassador for Lofted Spirits and Kentucky bourbon.

The appointment connects a familiar production team with a wider leadership remit. Its scope includes the company's own whiskey brands and its custom spirits business, rather than a single newly launched bottle.

Bardstown Reaches A Million-Barrel Milestone

The same announcement says Bardstown Bourbon Company has filled its one millionth barrel since distillation began in September 2016.

That is a cumulative production milestone. It is not a million bottles sold, nor a statement that every barrel has reached the same age or is ready for release. Barrel filling, maturation and a finished bottle are different stages of whiskey production.

How To Read The News As A Bourbon Drinker

A master-distiller appointment tells you who is responsible for production. By itself, it does not describe a particular whiskey's grain recipe, barrel selection or bottling strength, and it is not a tasting score.

For followers of Bardstown and Green River, Smith's promotion is a useful name to recognise in future releases. When choosing a bottle, keep the expression's age, proof and stated production details in view. The people behind a whiskey matter; the liquid still deserves its own assessment.

posts.title: Bottled-in-Bond Bourbon: Age, Proof And Serving Explained
posts.excerpt: Bottled-in-bond bourbon means more than 100 proof. Understand the four-year minimum, distilling-season rule and how it differs from straight bourbon.
posts.meta_description: Decode bottled-in-bond bourbon: four-year minimum, 100 proof and one distilling season. Find serving tips, Indian pairings and city prices on BevOry.
posts.selection_note: A focused American-whiskey label guide, chosen after the live catalogue showed an existing bourbon-versus-Scotch article; no duplicate broad comparison is added.
posts.content:
Bottled-in-bond bourbon is American bourbon that meets additional rules for production, ageing and bottling strength. It is bottled at exactly 100 US proof, or 50% ABV, and must be at least four years old. The term tells you more than the alcohol strength alone.

What The Label Guarantees

Under 27 CFR 5.88, bonded spirits must come from the same distiller, distillery and distilling season, using the same class of materials. The rule also sets the four-year storage minimum and exactly 50% ABV at bottling. For American products, the label identifies the distillery and the production and bottling plant numbers.

One distilling season means January-June or July-December, as Heaven Hill's bottled-in-bond guide explains. It does not mean the whiskey must come from only one barrel.

Straight Bourbon Is A Different Claim

American bourbon must use a grain mash containing at least 51% corn and be stored in new charred oak. Straight bourbon has a minimum two-year ageing requirement. The US whisky standards set out those distinctions.

So straight bourbon alone does not promise four years of ageing, a single distilling season or 100 proof. Equally, a bottle marked 100 proof is not automatically bottled-in-bond. Strength is only one part of the bonded designation.

What 100 Proof Does Not Mean

It means 50% alcohol by volume, not 100% alcohol. It is also not a score for quality or a guarantee that the whiskey will taste sweeter, smoother or better than another bourbon. Start with the specific expression's flavours and the way you plan to serve it.

A Concrete Bottle Example

Evan Williams Bottled-in-Bond is a four-year-old, 100-proof bourbon. Its producer describes caramel, vanilla and oak aromas, followed by citrus and black pepper on the palate, with a long, warm, dry finish. Those notes belong to this expression, not to every bonded whiskey.

Serving And Indian Food Pairings

Begin with a small neat pour in a tulip-shaped tasting glass. Add a few drops of water and taste again; the Evan Williams serving suggestion also takes this approach. For an everyday bonded bourbon, a rocks glass or a measured Old Fashioned is another practical option.

Our pairing suggestions for a caramel-and-spice bourbon are mutton seekh kebabs, mushroom tikka, grilled lamb chops, roasted almonds and 70% dark chocolate. Keep the chilli moderate at first so you can judge the match.

Comparing Prices In India

On BevOry, select Mumbai, Delhi, Gurgaon, Bengaluru or your own city. Match the exact bonded expression and bottle size. Do not substitute a price for the same brand's standard bottling: the labels describe different buying choices.
